title: How to use this site
text:
Every example on this site is written twice: once in R and once in Python. Both give the same answer. Click a tab to choose. The site remembers your choice on every page, so you only pick once.
Here is a tiny example: five pretend patients’ ages, their mean, and their standard deviation (SD).

RPython



ages <- c(64, 71, 58, 69, 75)   # five pretend patients' ages

mean_age <- mean(ages)           # the average
sd_age <- sd(ages)               # the standard deviation

mean_age

[1] 67.4

sd_age

[1] 6.580274





import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([64, 71, 58, 69, 75])   # five pretend patients' ages

mean_age = ages.mean()                    # the average
sd_age = ages.std()                       # the standard deviation

print(mean_age)

67.4

print(sd_age)

6.580273550544841





Both say the mean age is 67.4 years with an SD of 6.6 years.






Tip🔀 R vs Python: the standard deviation trap



Python has two common ways to compute an SD, and they disagree. pandas (ages.std()) divides by n − 1, like R’s sd(). numpy (np.std(ages)) divides by n unless you write np.std(ages, ddof=1). Medical papers report the n − 1 version. Whenever the two languages’ defaults differ, this site sets them explicitly and explains why in a box like this one.


Behind the scenes, every page checks that the R and Python answers match. If they ever disagree, the site refuses to build, so you can trust that both tabs say the same thing.

title: How to use this site
text:
Running the code yourself

Open the repository folder in Positron (see Install & set up).
Save practice files in the scratch/ folder, for example scratch/practice.R or scratch/practice.py. Git ignores everything in scratch/, so practice files can never be committed by accident.
Copy code with the copy button that appears in the top-right corner of every code block.
Run a line with Cmd+Enter (Mac) or Ctrl+Enter (Windows). Positron sends it to the console.

Data paths such as data/cohort.csv are relative to the repository’s top folder. Positron starts there when you open the folder, so the paths just work.

title: Working with real TJS data
text: Everything on this site uses invented data. Your real project won’t. This page covers the rules that keep patients and TJS safe. Read it before you open any real dataset.

title: Working with real TJS data
section: What counts as protected health information (PHI)
text:
What counts as protected health information (PHI)
US law (HIPAA) lists 18 kinds of identifiers. A dataset is only “de-identified” under the Safe Harbor method when all 18 are removed:


Names
Geographic units smaller than a state: street address, city, county, and ZIP code. The first three digits of a ZIP code may stay if that area holds more than 20,000 people.
All parts of dates except the year, when they relate to the patient: birth, admission, discharge, surgery, and death dates. For patients older than 89, remove every part of every date that reveals their age, including the year (so no birth year), and group their ages as “90 or older”.
Telephone numbers
Fax numbers
Email addresses
Social Security numbers
Medical record numbers (MRNs)
Health plan beneficiary numbers
Account numbers
Certificate or license numbers
Vehicle identifiers and serial numbers, including license plates
Device identifiers and serial numbers, including implant serial and lot numbers
Web addresses (URLs)
IP addresses
Biometric identifiers, such as fingerprints and voice prints
Full-face photographs and comparable images
Any other unique identifying number, characteristic, or code


These identifiers must also be removed for the patient’s relatives, employers, or household members. And Safe Harbor only counts if you have no actual knowledge that what’s left could still identify someone.

title: Working with real TJS data
text:
TJS-specific traps

Surgery dates are dates. Use “days from surgery” or the surgery year instead.
Ages over 89. Report them as “90 or older”, and drop the birth year and any other date that reveals their age.
Study IDs built from patient details. A study ID made from initials, an MRN, or a birth date (like JS-0412) is still an identifier. Use arbitrary codes such as C0001.
MRNs hide in file names. Watch for names like 12345678_xray.png or chart_pull_MRN.xlsx.
Implant stickers. Lot and serial numbers are device identifiers.
Radiographs. DICOM files carry the patient’s name, MRN and dates in their headers, and some images have them burned into the pixels.
Free-text “notes” columns. They collect names, phone numbers and dates.
Screenshots of the chart. They’re PHI too.

title: Working with real TJS data
text:
Where TJS data lives

Study data lives in TJS-controlled Google Sheets and Google Drive folders that your project lead shares with your TJS account.
Project repositories read data at run time, either straight from the Google Sheet or from a local data/ folder that is listed in .gitignore before the first commit.
The crosswalk that links MRNs to study IDs lives only with the data, never in a repository.
What leaves the secure environment is aggregate: tables, figures and model results. Your IRB protocol may require hiding small counts (for example, cells with fewer than 11 patients).

title: Working with real TJS data
section: How TJS projects handle data in code
text:
How TJS projects handle data in code
These rules come from TJS project repositories. Tidy data practices each one.

Read everything as text at first. Dates arrive in several formats, numbers contain stray text, and lists sit inside single cells. Convert types as a deliberate, recorded step, never silently while reading.
Match columns by name, not position. Two tabs of the same sheet can have different columns.
Check what you changed. After every cleaning step, compare row counts and summaries before and after.

title: Working with real TJS data
text:
AI tools
Never paste real patient data into an AI chatbot or any website. That includes ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and online “data cleaners”. The only exception is a tool your project lead confirms is approved for PHI. The synthetic data on this site is fine to paste anywhere.

title: Working with real TJS data
text:
Before every commit
Run these two commands and read the output:
git status
git diff --staged
Check that no data file, export or screenshot is listed. If you see one, unstage it with git restore --staged <file>.

title: Working with real TJS data
text:
If something goes wrong
If PHI reaches a commit, a push or an issue:

Stop. Don’t try to fix it with another commit. Git keeps the history.
Tell your project lead right away. The data has to be purged from history, and the incident may need to be reported under TJS policy.

Reporting quickly is always the right call, and nobody will be upset that you did.

title: TJS Statistics Tutorials
text:
New to statistics?
Work through the site in order: Getting started, then Part 1 · Foundations, then the catalog pages your project needs. Each page ends with short exercises and hidden solutions.

title: Install & set up
text: This takes 30–45 minutes the first time, and you only do it once per computer. Follow the steps in order. Each step ends with a quick check.

title: Install & set up
text:
1. Install R

Go to https://cloud.r-project.org.
Click Download R for macOS or Download R for Windows.

Mac: pick the installer for your chip. Apple menu → About This Mac: “Apple M…” means Apple silicon (arm64), and “Intel” means Intel (x86_64).
Windows: click base, then the download link at the top of the page.

Open the downloaded file and accept the defaults.

Check: Positron will find R in step 4. On a Mac you can also open Terminal and type R --version.

title: Install & set up
text:
2. Install uv and Python
Mac: open Terminal and run:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Windows: open PowerShell and run:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Close the window, open a new one, and install Python:
uv python install 3.13
Check: uv --version prints a version number.

title: Install & set up
text:
3. Install Git

Mac: in Terminal, run xcode-select --install and click Install. This installs Apple’s command-line tools, which include Git.
Windows: download Git from https://git-scm.com/downloads and accept the defaults.

Check: git --version prints a version number.

title: Install & set up
text:
4. Install Positron
Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co and install it like any other app. Positron runs R and Python side by side. Prefer RStudio or VS Code? See Other editors.

title: Install & set up
text:
5. Get this repository
In Terminal (Mac) or PowerShell (Windows), make a projects folder and download (“clone”) the repository into it:
mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
git clone https://github.com/Total-Joint-Specialists/example-stats-analysis.git
Use a folder that is not synced to the cloud. Documents and Desktop are often synced by iCloud (Mac) or OneDrive (Windows). Syncing slows down, and can break, the R and Python environments that steps 6 and 7 create.
Then, in Positron: File → Open Folder… and choose example-stats-analysis.

title: Install & set up
text:
6. Install the R packages
In Positron, start an R console: use the language picker at the top right of the Console pane and choose R. Because R starts inside the repository folder, it switches on this project’s package list. Then run:
renv::restore()
Answer Y if asked. This installs every R package the tutorials use, at the exact versions we tested. It takes a few minutes.

title: Install & set up
text:
7. Install the Python packages
Open Positron’s terminal (Terminal → New Terminal). It opens in the repository folder. Run:
uv sync
This creates a private Python environment in the .venv folder with every package the tutorials use. Then tell Positron to use it: in the Console pane’s language picker, choose the Python whose path includes .venv.

title: Install & set up
text:
8. Check that everything works
In Positron’s terminal, run both checks:
Rscript getting-started/check_setup.R
uv run python getting-started/check_setup.py
Each check ends with All good - you are ready. If a line says PROBLEM, it tells you what to do. Fix it and run the check again.
On Windows, if Rscript is “not recognized”, run the R check from Positron’s R console instead:
source("getting-started/check_setup.R")

title: Install & set up
text:
Reading the data without cloning
You can skip step 5 (cloning) and read the practice data straight from GitHub. You still need the packages, so install them first.

RPython


install.packages(c("readr", "readxl"))   # once

cohort <- readr::read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Total-Joint-Specialists/example-stats-analysis/main/data/cohort.csv")


Start Python with the packages it needs. In a terminal:
uv run --with pandas --with openpyxl python
Then:
import pandas as pd

cohort = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Total-Joint-Specialists/example-stats-analysis/main/data/cohort.csv")



Every CSV works the same way. In any example, replace "data/" with "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Total-Joint-Specialists/example-stats-analysis/main/data/".
Excel files are different. R’s read_excel() can’t read a web address, so download the file first. Python’s pd.read_excel() can read the address directly.

RPython


url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Total-Joint-Specialists/example-stats-analysis/main/data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(url, path, mode = "wb")   # "wb" keeps the file intact on Windows
site_a <- readxl::read_excel(path, sheet = "Site A")


url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Total-Joint-Specialists/example-stats-analysis/main/data/messy_abstraction_workbook.xlsx"
site_a = pd.read_excel(url, sheet_name="Site A")

title: Install & set up
text:
Troubleshooting







You see
Do this




You have not agreed to the Xcode license (Mac, during renv::restore())
In Terminal, run sudo xcodebuild -license accept and type your Mac password. Then run renv::restore() again.


there is no package called 'renv'
In the R console, run install.packages("renv"). Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run renv::restore() again.


uv: command not found, or “not recognized”
Close the terminal window, open a new one, and try again.


git: command not found
Repeat step 3.


Python can’t find pandas in Positron
Choose the .venv Python in the Console language picker (step 7), then restart the console.


Anything else
Copy the whole error message and send it to your TJS project lead.

title: Install & set up
text:
Other editors

RStudio (https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) is great for R. It can run Python too, but Positron is simpler when you use both.
VS Code (https://code.visualstudio.com) works too: install the R and Python extensions.

Everything else on this page stays the same.
